source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Libya
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: In Niger, Kel Tamasheq (Tuareg) herders raise camels and goats in Agadez, Tahoua and Tillabéry. Estimates for 2009 put them at about 1.2 million, 8.3% of the population.

source.title: Indigenous World 2020: Niger
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Endorois
nations.lands: around Lake Bogoria in Baringo County, and in Nakuru and Laikipia counties, in Kenya's Rift Valley

facts.text: The Endorois Welfare Council, founded in 1995 by senior members of the community, works for justice and sustainable development for the Endorois.

source.title: Endorois Welfare Council - Endorois Welfare Council for marginalized communities

facts.text: In 2010 the African Union approved an African Commission ruling in the Endorois case, the first in Africa to recognize Indigenous peoples' rights to land they traditionally owned.

source.title: Landmark decision rules Kenya’s removal of indigenous people from ancestral land illegal

nations.name: Yiaku
nations.lands: Mukogodo Forest in Laikipia County, Kenya

facts.text: Yiaku women and elders now lead language teaching and forest care, and growing youth involvement is strengthening the community.

source.title: Reviving Indigenous forest stewardship
source.publisher: International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)

facts.text: Since 2003 the Yiaku Laikipiak Trust has worked to protect Mukogodo Forest and keep Yiaku culture alive.

source.title: Reviving Indigenous forest stewardship
source.publisher: International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)

nations.name: Anywaa
nations.lands: Gambella in western Ethiopia, along the Akobo, Alwaro, Openo (Baro) and Gilo rivers, and neighbouring South Sudan

facts.text: Anywaa activists helped found EMIPRO in 2022, the first legally registered Indigenous-led rights organization in Ethiopia.

source.title: “We Belong to This Land:” The Anywaa Peoples’ Fight for Survival, Dignity, and Recognition in Ethiopia

facts.text: The Anywaa are river farmers and fishers whose lives follow the Akobo, Alwaro, Openo (Baro) and Gilo rivers of Gambella.

source.title: “We Belong to This Land:” The Anywaa Peoples’ Fight for Survival, Dignity, and Recognition in Ethiopia

nations.name: Toubou
nations.lands: the Tibesti plateau of northern Chad, southern Libya along the Chad border, and northern Niger

facts.text: Toubou herders practise mobile pastoralism across a wide area stretching from northern Niger to Sudan.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Libya chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: About 50,000 Toubou live in Libya along the border with Chad; the people's origins lie in the Tibesti plateau.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Libya chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Rifians
nations.lands: the Rif of northern and north-eastern Morocco, including Al Hoceima province

facts.text: In Morocco's 2024 census, 53.6% of people in Al Hoceima province said they use Tarifit, the language of the Irifiyen.

source.title: RGPH 2024: Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, Région Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceima

facts.text: Nationwide, 3.2% of Morocco's population reported Tarifit among the local languages they use, in the 2024 census.

source.title: RGPH 2024: Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, Région Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceima

nations.name: Baka
nations.lands: forests of eastern and southern Cameroon, northern Gabon, and neighbouring parts of the Republic of the Congo and Central African Republic

facts.text: In Gabon, the Baka are one of nine Indigenous forest peoples, alongside the Babongo, Bakoya and others, each with its own language and culture.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Gabon chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: In 2025 a Batouri workshop run by the association ASBABUK and Cameroon's forestry ministry focused on fully recognizing Baka as rightful partners in managing forest resources.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Cameroon
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Sengwer
nations.lands: Cherangany Hills and Embobut Forest in Kenya's western highlands

facts.text: Sengwer society is organized around clans, each with its own roles, and elders guide decisions and teach younger generations.
Sengwer knowledge includes sustainable ways of hunting, gathering, beekeeping and caring for forest resources, which helps conserve biodiversity.

nations.name: Kabyles
nations.lands: Kabylia in north-eastern Algeria, with a large community in France

facts.text: Taqbaylit, the Kabyle language, is one of three Amazigh languages taught from bachelor's level to doctorate at Inalco in Paris.

source.title: Kabyle (Berber)
source.publisher: Inalco (Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales)

facts.text: Kabyles make up around half of Algeria's Amazigh population, centred on Kabylia in the north-east.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Algeria chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Mozabite
nations.lands: the M'Zab valley around Ghardaïa in the Algerian Sahara

facts.text: UNESCO credits the M'Zab with an ingenious system for capturing and sharing water which, with its palm groves, makes life work in a semi-desert.
The M'Zab valley habitat, built in the tenth century by the Ibadites around five ksour (fortified towns), survives intact and is UNESCO World Heritage.

nations.name: BaAka
nations.lands: forests between the Oubangui and Sangha rivers, in south-western Central African Republic and northern Republic of the Congo

facts.text: Dzanga-Sangha Protected Areas credits BaAka knowledge of the forest as central to its research, conservation and tourism work.
The Central African Republic, home to many BaAka communities, ratified ILO Convention 169 on Indigenous peoples in 2010, the first African state to do so.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2021: Central African Republic
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Muskeg Lake Cree Nation
nations.lands: Treaty 6 territory in central Saskatchewan, Canada, with urban reserve land in Saskatoon

facts.text: Muskeg Lake Cree Nation planned a gathering for August 20 to 23, 2026 to mark 150 years since Treaty 6 was signed.

source.title: Muskeg Lake Cree Nation, Band No. 102

facts.text: In 1988 Muskeg Lake Cree Nation created Asimakeniseekan Askiy in Saskatoon, the first commercial urban reserve in Canada.

nations.name: Gitxsan
nations.lands: The Laxyip along the upper Skeena River and its tributaries in northern British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: Gitxsan society is matriarchal, with four clans made up of independent Houses (Huwilp), each led by a Wii Simoogit, or high chief.
Gitxsanimaax, the traditional Gitxsan language, has two dialects: Giigeenix, spoken up river, and Gyeets, spoken down river.

nations.name: Piikani Nation
nations.lands: Around Brocket in southern Alberta, Canada, near the Old Man River; part of the Blackfoot Confederacy

facts.text: Piikani stories, ceremonies and songs describe an ancestral territory reaching north to the North Saskatchewan River and west into the Rocky Mountains.
Piikani Nation had 3,928 registered members as of September 2026.

source.title: First Nation Profiles: Registered Population (Piikani Nation)
source.publisher: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada

nations.name: Atikamekw
nations.lands: Nitaskinan in central Quebec, Canada, with the communities of Manawan, Wemotaci and Opitciwan

facts.text: The Atikamekw language, like other Algonquin and Anishinaabe languages, is rich in imagery and names things by how they truly are.
Young people aged 0 to 35 make up about 65 percent of the Atikamekw population today.

nations.name: Innu
nations.lands: Nitassinan: Labrador (Newfoundland and Labrador) and eastern Quebec, Canada

facts.text: In 2008 the Innu Nation and Newfoundland and Labrador signed the Tshash Petapen, or New Dawn, Agreement.

source.title: Innu Nation of Labrador
source.publisher: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, Indigenous Affairs and Reconciliation

facts.text: The Innu Nation land claim, accepted for negotiation in 1978, covers about 70 percent of Labrador.

source.title: Innu Nation of Labrador
source.publisher: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, Indigenous Affairs and Reconciliation

nations.name: Six Nations of the Grand River
nations.lands: Along the Grand River in southern Ontario, Canada

facts.text: It is the only First Nation community home to all six Haudenosaunee nations: Mohawk, Cayuga, Onondaga, Oneida, Seneca and Tuscarora.

source.title: Who We Are
source.publisher: Six Nations of the Grand River

facts.text: No First Nation in Canada has a larger population than Six Nations of the Grand River.

source.title: Who We Are
source.publisher: Six Nations of the Grand River

nations.name: Haíɫzaqv
nations.lands: The Central Coast of British Columbia, Canada, centred on Bella Bella (Wáglísla) on Campbell Island

facts.text: In 2025 Heiltsuk members ratified a written constitution, a milestone in self-governance.
Haíɫzaqv means 'to speak and act correctly', principles that guide Heiltsuk ancestral and present-day ways of life.

nations.name: Tłı̨chǫ
nations.lands: Between Great Slave Lake and Great Bear Lake in the Northwest Territories, Canada, around the communities of Behchokǫ̀, Whatì, Gamètì and Wekweètì

facts.text: The Tłı̨chǫ Agreement, in effect since August 4, 2005, was the first combined land, resources and self-government agreement in the Northwest Territories.

source.title: Concluding and Implementing Land and Resources and Self-Government Agreements: Tłı̨chǫ
source.publisher: Government of the Northwest Territories, Executive and Indigenous Affairs

facts.text: The Tłı̨chǫ Government makes laws for its citizens in areas including education, child and family services, and Tłı̨chǫ language and culture.

source.title: Concluding and Implementing Land and Resources and Self-Government Agreements: Tłı̨chǫ
source.publisher: Government of the Northwest Territories, Executive and Indigenous Affairs

nations.name: xʷməθkʷəy̓əm
nations.lands: The Fraser River estuary, including much of Metro Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: Musqueam is a strong, growing community of more than 1,300 members, many living on the Musqueam reserve near the mouth of the Fraser River.
The name xʷməθkʷəy̓əm means place of the məθkʷəy̓, a plant, and Musqueam people are traditionally hən̓q̓əmin̓əm̓ speakers.

nations.name: Inuvialuit
nations.lands: The Inuvialuit Settlement Region in the western Arctic, Northwest Territories and Yukon, Canada

facts.text: Six communities lie within the Inuvialuit Settlement Region: Aklavik, Inuvik, Paulatuk, Sachs Harbour, Tuktoyaktuk and Ulukhaktok.
One of the agreement's basic goals is keeping Inuvialuit cultural identity and values strong as northern society changes.

nations.name: Kainai
nations.lands: Southern Alberta, Canada, with its main community at Standoff; part of the Blackfoot Confederacy

facts.text: The Blood Tribe's stated mission is to preserve and protect its lands, culture, language and traditions in the spirit of Kainayssini.
In 2026 the Blood Tribe Land Management Department won a Prairie Conservation Award.

nations.name: Eeyou
also: Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee)
nations.lands: Eeyou Istchee, the lands east of James Bay and Hudson Bay in northern Quebec, Canada

facts.text: Each Eeyou First Nation runs its own local government, and every elected Chief also sits on the board of the Grand Council of the Crees to address shared issues.

source.title: The Eeyou of Eeyou Istchee
source.publisher: Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee) / Cree Nation Government

facts.text: Eeyou Istchee is home to more than 20,000 people.

source.title: The Eeyou of Eeyou Istchee
source.publisher: Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee) / Cree Nation Government

nations.name: Nation Wendat
nations.lands: Wendake, near Québec City, within the traditional territory Onyionhwentsïio’ in Quebec, Canada

facts.text: After the Wendat language went dormant in the 1800s, the Yawenda project (2007 to 2012) brought language specialists and community members together to revive it.
The Nation counts more than 300 Wendat businesses, including many artisans, artists and cultural organizations.

nations.name: səlilwətaɬ
nations.lands: Burrard Inlet (səlilwət) in North Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: Tsleil-Waututh people see caring for the lands and waters of their territory as a birthright and obligation, so future generations can thrive.
Tsleil-Waututh means 'People of the Inlet'. The Nation's language is hən̓q̓əmin̓əm, in which its name is səlilwətaɬ.

nations.name: Akwesasne
nations.lands: Along the St. Lawrence River where Ontario, Quebec and New York State meet, in Canada and the United States

facts.text: Akwesasne spans lands in Quebec, Ontario and New York State, and three separate but linked political bodies govern it.
Kanien'kéha, the Mohawk language, remains central to identity in Akwesasne and is actively taught in its schools.

nations.name: Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw
nations.lands: The North Shore of Vancouver and the Squamish River valley, British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: The Nation's roots lie in several communities that became one government in 1923. Most members live on Vancouver's North Shore, others along the Squamish River.
The Squamish language is a sign of resilience: dozens of Nation members are learning it from their Elders as a second language.

nations.name: Haida Nation
nations.lands: Haida Gwaii, an archipelago off the north coast of British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: The Council of the Haida Nation works to steward the lands and waters of Haida territories and carry Haida culture and language to future generations.
In April 2024 British Columbia and the Council of the Haida Nation signed the Rising Tide agreement, a first of its kind recognizing Haida Aboriginal title in Haida Gwaii.

source.title: For Immediate Release: Haida Nation, B.C. recognize Haida Aboriginal title, a historic first in Canada

nations.name: Mescalero Apache
nations.lands: South-central New Mexico, US (Mescalero Apache Reservation)

facts.text: Today three peoples, the Mescalero, Lipan and Chiricahua Apache, together make up the Mescalero Apache Tribe on a 463,000 acre reservation.
The Mescalero Apache Tribe owns and runs the Inn of the Mountain Gods Resort and the Ski Apache ski area.

source.title: Official Website of the Mescalero Apache Tribe

nations.name: Jicarilla Apache
nations.lands: North-central New Mexico, US, along the Colorado line and across the Continental Divide (Dulce)

facts.text: The Jicarilla Apache Nation reservation spans more than 879,917 acres in north-central New Mexico, and Dulce is its only community and tribal headquarters.
After 1887 the Jicarilla moved their individual allotments back into tribal ownership, keeping their lands and water rights together.

nations.name: Akimel O’otham
nations.lands: Gila River Indian Community, south of Phoenix, Arizona, US, shared with the Pee Posh (Maricopa)

facts.text: The Akimel O’otham welcomed the Pee Posh (Maricopa) to the Gila River long ago, and the two peoples still share its lands and resources today.
Akimel O’otham basket weaving is in revival, and in 2004 the community dedicated the Huhugam Heritage Center to care for its heritage.

nations.name: Yoreme
nations.lands: Southern Sonora (Etchojoa, Huatabampo, Navojoa) and northern Sinaloa (Ahome, El Fuerte, Guasave), Mexico

facts.text: Yoreme communities have traditional governors. In December 2025 they met Mexico’s federal agrarian office to set a path for continuing the Yoreme-Mayo Justice Plan.

source.title: Atienden Plan de Justicia al pueblo Yoreme-Mayo de Sonora

facts.text: Yoreme patron saint fiestas strengthen the social networks that link communities across Mayo lands and keep Yoreme identity alive.

source.title: Mayos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Ute Mountain Ute Tribe
nations.lands: Towaoc and reservation lands in southwestern Colorado and northwestern New Mexico; White Mesa, Utah, United States

facts.text: The Ute Mountain Ute Tribe identifies itself as the Weenuche band of the Ute Nation, with its tribal offices in Towaoc, Colorado.
White Mesa Administration supports community members with employment, education and access to basic services in White Mesa, Utah.

nations.name: Comcaac
nations.lands: Desert coast of Sonora on the Gulf of California, Mexico, including Punta Chueca, El Desemboque and Tiburón Island

facts.text: In 1975 Mexico declared the Canal del Infiernillo an exclusive Comcaac fishing zone and symbolically granted them Tiburón Island, a nature reserve, as communal land.

source.title: Seris
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: Comcaac artisans weave coritas, baskets made since before Spanish contact. A very large one can take a year or two to finish.

source.title: Seris
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Hualapai
nations.lands: Northwestern Arizona, US, along the Grand Canyon and Colorado River (Peach Springs)

facts.text: The name Hualapai means People of the Tall Pines.
The Hualapai Reservation, set up in 1883, covers about one million acres along 108 miles of the Grand Canyon and Colorado River.

nations.name: Warihó and Macurawe
nations.lands: Foothills of the Sierra Madre Occidental on the Chihuahua and Sonora border, Mexico

facts.text: The people call themselves Macurawe in Sonora and Warihó in Chihuahua. Their Uto-Aztecan language has two variants and bridges Tarahumara and Mayo.

source.title: Guarijíos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: Warihó and Macurawe families weave baskets, mats and hats from palm and fiber and build harps, violins and guitars. Their craft work is family based and rests with women.

source.title: Guarijíos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Diné
nations.lands: Diné Bikéyah (Navajoland) across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, US

facts.text: The Navajo Nation Council, the Nation’s governing body, has 24 delegates elected from legislative districts.
Diné Bikéyah, the Navajo Nation, covers more than 27,000 square miles across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, larger than 10 of the 50 US states.

nations.name: Havasu Baaja
nations.lands: Havasu Canyon in the Grand Canyon, Arizona, US (village of Supai)

facts.text: Supai is so remote that the US Postal Service carries all mail in and out of the canyon by mule train.
The Havasupai reservation was set up in 1880 and greatly enlarged in 1975. It covers 188,077 acres beside the South Rim of the Grand Canyon.

nations.name: White Mountain Apache
nations.lands: White Mountains of east-central Arizona, US (Fort Apache Indian Reservation, Whiteriver)

facts.text: The White Mountain Apache own and run Sunrise, one of the largest ski resorts in the Southwest, and rare Apache trout swim in reservation streams.
White Mountain Apache people live on 1.6 million acres of their ancestral homeland, the Fort Apache Indian Reservation, set aside in 1891.

nations.name: Tonto Apache Tribe
nations.lands: Payson, Gila County, Arizona, United States

facts.text: The Tonto Apache Tribe is based beside Payson in northwestern Gila County, Arizona.
In 2010, land for the Tonto Apache Tribe was acquired in trust following a land exchange with the U.S. Forest Service.

source.title: Reservation proclamation for trust land belonging to the Tonto Apache Tribe of Arizona

nations.name: Yavapai
nations.lands: Central and western Arizona, US, including Fort McDowell near Phoenix and Prescott

facts.text: In September 2026 the Fort McDowell Yavapai Nation, about 950 members, marked 123 years since its land was set aside in 1903.

source.title: Welcome to Fort McDowell Yavapai Nation

facts.text: In 1976 Fort McDowell Yavapai community members voted 144 to 57 against selling their land for the Orme Dam, and in 1981 the dam was called off.

nations.name: Ohkay Owingeh
nations.lands: Where the Rio Grande and Rio Chama meet, northern New Mexico, US

facts.text: Ohkay Owingeh is the headquarters of the Eight Northern Pueblo Tribal Council.
The people have long called their home Ohkay Owingeh, place of the strong people in Tewa, and officially restored that name in place of San Juan, given in 1598.

nations.name: Cocopah
nations.lands: Lower Colorado River and delta: south of Yuma and near Somerton, Arizona, US, and the Mexicali valley of Baja California and San Luis Río Colorado, Sonora, Mexico

facts.text: About 1,000 Cocopah tribal members live and work on or near their reservation south of Yuma, Arizona, which was established in 1917.
Since 2003 the Cucapá of El Mayor, Baja California, and the Cocopah of Somerton, Arizona, have met each year with dances, songs, crafts and food.

source.title: Cucapás
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Nuche
nations.lands: Southwestern Colorado (Ignacio, Towaoc), northeastern Utah (Uintah and Ouray) and nearby New Mexico and Utah lands, US

facts.text: There are three Ute tribes today: the Southern Ute (Mouache and Capote bands), the Ute Mountain Ute (Weenuche band) and the Northern Ute in Utah.
The Ute Mountain Ute Tribe teaches the Ute language to Head Start children ages 2 to 5 and holds evening language classes for adults.

nations.name: Baniwa
nations.lands: Içana river and the Upper Rio Negro in Amazonas, Brazil, and neighboring Colombia and Venezuela

facts.text: The Baniwa speak languages of the Arawak family along the Içana river.
Baniwa communities live where Brazil meets Colombia and Venezuela, along the Içana river in the Upper Rio Negro region.

nations.name: Wapichana
nations.lands: Northeastern Roraima, Brazil, and the South Rupununi in southwestern Guyana

facts.text: In 2012 Wapichan leaders in Guyana presented a community map and land plan titled Thinking Together for those Coming Behind Us.

source.title: Wapichan people in Guyana present territorial map and community proposals to save ancestral forests

facts.text: The Wapichana language is classified in the Arawak language family.

nations.name: Guarani Mbya
nations.lands: Villages across southern and southeastern Brazil, eastern Paraguay, Misiones province in Argentina, and near Montevideo in Uruguay

facts.text: The Comissão Guarani Yvyrupa, founded in 2006, brings together Guarani collectives in six states of southern and southeastern Brazil.
In Guarani, yvyrupa names the structure that holds up the land, recalling free movement across territory before today's borders.

nations.name: Sápara
nations.lands: Rainforest of Pastaza province in the Ecuadorian Amazon, straddling the border with Peru

facts.text: The Sápara live in a part of the Amazon rainforest that straddles Ecuador and Peru.

source.title: Oral heritage and cultural manifestations of the Zápara people

facts.text: Sápara knowledge of the forest shows in their rich vocabulary for plants and animals and in their knowledge of the forest's medicinal plants.

source.title: Oral heritage and cultural manifestations of the Zápara people

nations.name: Kuikuro
nations.lands: Upper Xingu, in the Xingu Indigenous Territory, Mato Grosso, Brazil

facts.text: Kuikuro is a southern Carib language.
Kuikuro remains a living, intact language, used by everyone in all domains except talking with outsiders.

nations.name: Ka'apor
nations.lands: Northern Maranhão, Brazil, in the Alto Turiaçu Indigenous Land

facts.text: Ka'apor communities have had a shared, standard sign language for communicating with deaf members of the community.
Ka'apor is a language of the Tupi-Guarani family.

nations.name: A'uwe
nations.lands: Eastern Mato Grosso, Brazil, in Indigenous lands such as Pimentel Barbosa, Marãiwatsédé, São Marcos and Sangradouro

facts.text: The A'uwe (Xavante) language belongs to the Jê family of the Macro-Jê language stock.
The Xavante numbered about 22,256 people in 2020.

nations.name: Pataxó
nations.lands: Villages in the far south of Bahia and the north of Minas Gerais, Brazil

facts.text: The Pataxó are rebuilding their language, Patxohã, through a major community effort.
Pataxó villages are spread across the far south of Bahia and the north of Minas Gerais.

nations.name: Macuxi
nations.lands: Fields and mountains of northern Roraima, Brazil, between the headwaters of the Branco and Rupununi rivers, extending into Guyana and Venezuela

facts.text: The Conselho Indígena de Roraima, founded in 1990, unites ten peoples including the Macuxi and Wapichana, with 270 of the state's 465 communities as members.
The Macuxi language belongs to the Carib language family.

nations.name: Ashaninka
nations.lands: Upper Juruá region of Acre, Brazil, including the Amônia, Breu and Envira rivers, near the Peruvian border

facts.text: Ashaninka of the Amônia river created their own association, Apiwtxa, in 1991; it was officially registered in 1993.
Ashenĩka, the people's own name, can be translated as my relatives, my folk or my people.

nations.name: Terena
nations.lands: Mato Grosso do Sul, with communities in Mato Grosso and São Paulo, Brazil

facts.text: Farming remains the main productive activity in Terena reserves.
Terena people living in cities are concentrated mainly in Campo Grande, and most of them keep strong ties with their reserves.

nations.name: Tikuna
nations.lands: Along the upper Solimões (Amazon) river in Amazonas, Brazil, and in neighboring Peru and Colombia

facts.text: Tikuna communities are spread across three countries: Brazil, Peru and Colombia.
Tikuna is a tonal language, considered genetically isolated, with a complex sound system and grammar.

nations.name: Shuar
nations.lands: Zamora Chinchipe, Morona Santiago and southern Pastaza provinces in the Ecuadorian Amazon

facts.text: In 2022 the Shuar Aratsim Center approved its own Life Plan after participatory community workshops.

source.title: Territory of the Shuar People
source.publisher: ReVista, Harvard Review of Latin America (David Rockefeller Center for Latin American Studies)

facts.text: The Interprovincial Federation of Shuar Centers (FICSH), founded in 1964, was one of the pioneering Indigenous organizations of the Amazon.

source.title: Territory of the Shuar People
source.publisher: ReVista, Harvard Review of Latin America (David Rockefeller Center for Latin American Studies)

nations.name: Achuar
nations.lands: Northern Loreto in Peru near the Ecuador border, and the neighboring Amazon of Ecuador

facts.text: Peru's Ministry of Culture has registered five interpreters and translators of the Achuar language.

source.title: Achuar | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: Achuar is a cross-border language, spoken in both Peru and Ecuador.

source.title: Achuar | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Avá Guarani
nations.lands: Mato Grosso do Sul and Paraná in Brazil, and eastern Paraguay

facts.text: Guarani peoples, the Avá Guarani among them, live across a territory that spans regions of Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina.
The Avá Guarani, called Ñandeva in Brazil, have a present-day territory that takes in parts of Mato Grosso do Sul and Paraná.

source.title: Guarani Kaiowá - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

nations.name: Wounaan
nations.lands: Darién and eastern Panama, including the Emberá-Wounaan comarca and collective lands, and the San Juan River region of Colombia

facts.text: Wounaan forest technicians map illegal clearing with smartphone apps and GIS, and communities bring that evidence to the Wounaan National Congress.

source.title: Panama's Indigenous Groups Wage High-Tech Fight for Their Lands
source.publisher: Yale Environment 360, Yale School of the Environment

facts.text: Panama's 2023 census counted 10,634 Wounaan people.

source.title: Cuadro 20. Población indígena en la República, por sexo, según provincia, comarca indígena, grupo indígena al que pertenece y grupos de edad: Censo 2023
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama

nations.name: K'iche'
nations.lands: Western highlands of Guatemala, including Quiché, Totonicapán, Quetzaltenango and Sololá

facts.text: In Totonicapán, the 48 Cantones is a K'iche' ancestral authority built from community governments, with representatives chosen each year in assembly.

source.title: Former Indigenous authorities of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán released in Guatemala after more than a year in pretrial detention

facts.text: The 48 Cantones' system of caring for forests and water has served as an example for communities all over Guatemala.

nations.name: Q'eqchi'
nations.lands: Alta Verapaz, Izabal and Petén in Guatemala, and the Toledo District of southern Belize

facts.text: Radio Chiquixji in Alta Verapaz, Guatemala, broadcasts for bilingual Q'eqchi' and Spanish speakers and for communities that speak only Q'eqchi'.

source.title: Announcing Our 2019 Community Media Grants Partners

facts.text: In southern Belize, 39 Q'eqchi' and Mopan Maya communities have rights to their customary lands, as Belize's highest appeals court affirmed in 2015.

source.title: Maya Leaders Alliance Advocates at United Nations Urging Respect for Rule of Law in Belize

nations.name: Cabécar
nations.lands: Indigenous territories in the Talamanca mountains and Chirripó area of Costa Rica, in Limón, Cartago and Puntarenas provinces

facts.text: Costa Rica's 2011 census found that 87.6 percent of people in the official Cabécar territories speak the Cabécar language.
Costa Rica's 2013 list of Indigenous territories includes Cabécar territories such as Alto Chirripó, Bajo Chirripó, Talamanca Cabécar, Ujarrás and Telire.

source.title: Anexo 6: Pueblos y territorios indígenas de Costa Rica (2013)

nations.name: Buglé
nations.lands: The Ngäbe-Buglé comarca and nearby areas of Bocas del Toro and Veraguas in western Panama

facts.text: Under Panama's 1997 comarca law, the comarca's General Congress is the highest body for the ethnic and cultural voice and decisions of the Ngäbe-Buglé people.

source.title: Ley 10 de 7 de marzo de 1997, por la cual se crea la Comarca Ngöbe-Buglé
source.publisher: FAOLEX, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

facts.text: Panama's 2023 census counted 23,898 Buglé people; about 12,000 of them live in the Ngäbe-Buglé comarca, which they share with the Ngäbe.

source.title: Cuadro 20. Población indígena en la República, por sexo, según provincia, comarca indígena, grupo indígena al que pertenece y grupos de edad: Censo 2023
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama

nations.name: Naso Tjër Di
nations.lands: The Naso Tjër Di comarca along the Teribe River in Bocas del Toro, northwestern Panama, near the Costa Rican border

facts.text: The Naso are led by a king who lives in Sieyik, where Panama's president came in 2020 to sign the law creating their comarca.

source.title: Indigenous community wins recognition of its land rights in Panama

facts.text: In December 2020 Panama created the 1,600 square kilometer Naso Tjër Di comarca, the result of decades of Naso efforts to secure their land rights.

source.title: Indigenous community wins recognition of its land rights in Panama

nations.name: Mopan
nations.lands: The Toledo District of southern Belize and nearby Petén, Guatemala

facts.text: In 2022 a Free, Prior and Informed Consultation Protocol for the Maya of southern Belize was adopted, and in 2025 a working draft on protecting Maya customary land tenure followed.

source.title: Closing Remarks at the Final Monitoring Hearing in Maya Leaders v The Attorney General of Belize [2015] CCJ 15 (AJ)

facts.text: A 2015 Caribbean Court of Justice judgment obliges Belize's government to mark out and register Maya village lands in the south and guard them against outsiders.

source.title: Maya Q'eqchi and Mopan of Southern Belize Win Major Land Rights Victory in International Appeals Court (statement by the Maya Leaders Alliance)

nations.name: Miskitu
nations.lands: The Caribbean coast of Nicaragua and La Moskitia in northeastern Honduras, along the Wangki (Coco) River

facts.text: In 2021 the Yapti Tasba community radio network, linked to Miskitu organization YATAMA, reached 17 Indigenous territories and 154 communities, 95 percent of them Miskitu.

source.title: Pueblo Miskitu, YATAMA, and Yapti Tasba Radios Advance Indigenous Rights on the North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua

facts.text: Nicaragua's Caribbean Coast autonomy law affirms that Indigenous communities there have the right to keep and develop their languages and to bilingual education.

source.title: Pueblo Miskitu, YATAMA, and Yapti Tasba Radios Advance Indigenous Rights on the North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua

nations.name: Garifuna
nations.lands: Caribbean coast of Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua, plus large diaspora communities

facts.text: In 2024, Belize observed Garifuna Settlement Day on 19 November as one of its official public holidays.
Most Garifuna communities today are in Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua and Belize, and the Garifuna language is part of the Arawakan family.

source.title: Language, dance and music of the Garifuna

nations.name: Kalinago
nations.lands: The Kalinago Territory on the northeast coast of Dominica, in the eastern Caribbean

facts.text: In July 2024, voters in the Kalinago Territory elected their Kalinago Chief; the winning candidate received about 58 percent of the votes counted.
The Kalinago Territory has its own local government: a Chief and six councillors elected by residents every five years, alongside representation in Dominica's parliament.

source.title: The Kalinago Territory
source.publisher: Division of Culture, Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica

nations.name: Mayangna
nations.lands: The Bosawás region and North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua, with related Tawahka communities in Honduras

facts.text: After the 2020 hurricanes, Mayangna communities in Bonanza rebuilt together: they repaired 15 roofs collectively and planted 50 plots of grains, beans, corn and cassava.

source.title: Mayagna Communities Work to Achieve Food Sovereignty after Hurricanes Iota and Eta

facts.text: Nicaragua's Bosawás Biosphere Reserve, in the Mosquitia region, is ancestral territory of the Mayangna and Miskitu peoples, whose rights there are recognized.

source.title: Mayagna Communities Work to Achieve Food Sovereignty after Hurricanes Iota and Eta

nations.name: Lenca
nations.lands: Western and southwestern Honduras (Intibucá, Lempira, La Paz and nearby departments) and eastern El Salvador

facts.text: COPINH runs Lenca community radio stations that share news bulletins, podcasts, interviews and training with Lenca communities.

source.title: Las palabras haciendo eco en los caminos del pueblo Lenca: COPINH

facts.text: A community journalism program trained 24 Lenca women and 17 men as community correspondents, starting during the COVID-19 pandemic.

source.title: Indigenous, Garifuna, and Feminist Community Correspondents Push for a More Inclusive Democracy

nations.name: Xinka
nations.lands: Santa Rosa, Jutiapa and Jalapa departments in southeastern Guatemala

facts.text: In May 2024 the Parliament of the Xinka People hosted Guatemala's president in San Juan de Arana, Cuilapa, where they signed a 13-point work agenda.

source.title: Alegres le abrimos las puertas de nuestra casa, como usted nos ha abierto las puertas del Palacio, dice el pueblo xinca al presidente Arévalo

facts.text: In Santa Rosa, the Xinka People's Council (COPXIG), a local cooperative and the departmental education office work together to restore and teach the Xinka language.

source.title: Historia e Identidad del Pueblo Xinka
source.publisher: Universidad de San Carlos de Guatemala, Dirección General de Investigación

nations.name: Ch'ol
nations.lands: Northern Chiapas, Mexico, including Tila, Tumbalá, Palenque, Sabanilla and Salto de Agua

facts.text: La Voz de la Selva, a Chiapas public radio station on air since 2000 in Santo Domingo, Ocosingo, broadcasts in Spanish, Tseltal, Ch'ol and Lacandón.

source.title: XHSDM-FM La Voz de la Selva : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Maize is at the heart of Ch'ol culture, and many festivals follow the farming year, from preparing the fields and sowing to the harvest.

source.title: Ch'oles : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Tutunakú
nations.lands: The Totonacapan: northern Veracruz around Papantla and the Sierra Norte de Puebla, Mexico

facts.text: Community groups asked for radio in their own languages, and since 1994 La Voz de la Sierra Norte in Cuetzalan, Puebla has served Nahua and Totonac peoples.

source.title: XECTZ La Voz de la Sierra Norte (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: At the Centre for Indigenous Arts, Totonac is the language of teaching, and each art is taught in its own house-school, laid out like a traditional settlement.

source.title: Xtaxkgakget Makgkaxtlawana: the Centre for Indigenous Arts and its contribution to safeguarding the intangible cultural heritage of the Totonac people of Veracruz, Mexico

nations.name: Ayuuk
nations.lands: The Sierra Mixe of northeastern Oaxaca, Mexico, including Tlahuitoltepec, Tamazulapam, Ayutla and Guichicovi

facts.text: Backstrap loom weaving continues in Tamazulapam, Tlahuitoltepec and Cotzocón, and young Ayuuk artists are taking up mural and canvas painting.

source.title: Mixes : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

facts.text: In the Ayuuk language the word for a festival is xëëw, which also means day, sun, time and name.

source.title: Mixes : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Maya
nations.lands: Yucatán, Campeche and Quintana Roo, on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula

facts.text: La Voz de los Mayas, an INPI radio station broadcasting from Peto, Yucatán since 1982, reaches 677 localities across the peninsula in Maya and Spanish.

source.title: XEPET La Voz de los Mayas (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: In Felipe Carrillo Puerto, Quintana Roo, the INPI station La Voz del Gran Pueblo builds its programming with a citizen council of 25 people from 20 communities.

source.title: XHNKA La Voz del Gran Pueblo (FM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

nations.name: Tsa ju jmí'
nations.lands: La Chinantla in northeastern Oaxaca, Mexico, and resettled communities in Veracruz

facts.text: Since November 18, 1991, La Voz de la Chinantla, an INPI station in San Lucas Ojitlán, has broadcast with bilingual Chinantec, Mazatec and Cuicatec staff.

source.title: XEOJN La Voz de la Chinantla (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Chinantecs call themselves tsa ju jmí', people of the ancient word; each town also has its own name, beginning with tsa, dsa or alla, meaning people.

source.title: Chinantecos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Jñatrjo
nations.lands: The northwestern State of Mexico and eastern Michoacán, Mexico

facts.text: La Voz de la Sierra Oriente, on air since 1998 for Mazahua and Otomí communities, hosts poetry recitals and rock concerts in their own languages.

source.title: XETUX La Voz de la Sierra Oriente (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: In Mazahua and Otomí communities, their own normative systems guide shared work, forest care, land tenure and the election of community authorities.

source.title: XETUX La Voz de la Sierra Oriente (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

nations.name: Ha shuta enima
nations.lands: The Sierra Mazateca of northern Oaxaca around Huautla de Jiménez, Mexico, and nearby parts of Veracruz

facts.text: The sound archive of La Voz de la Chinantla, an INPI station in Oaxaca, holds over 5,000 music recordings, including Mazatec huehuentones musicians.

source.title: XEOJN La Voz de la Chinantla (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Mazatecs call themselves Ha shuta enima, which in their language means those who work the hills, humble people of custom.

source.title: Mazatecos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Triqui
nations.lands: Western Oaxaca, Mexico: a lower zone centered on San Juan Copala and an upper zone centered on San Andrés Chicahuaxtla

facts.text: La Voz de la Mixteca, an INPI radio station in Tlaxiaco, Oaxaca, broadcasts in Mixtec, Triqui and Spanish.

source.title: XETLA La Voz de la Mixteca (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: The name Triqui comes from driqui in the Triqui language, built from words meaning father and great or superior.

source.title: Triquis : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Nahua
nations.lands: Many states of central and southern Mexico, including Puebla, Veracruz, Hidalgo, Guerrero, San Luis Potosí, the State of Mexico, Morelos, Tlaxcala and Mexico City

facts.text: XEZON, an INPI radio station in the Sierra de Zongolica, Veracruz, serves Nahua communities; relatives working in the United States can hear family on its programs by phone.

source.title: XEZON La Voz de la Sierra de Zongolica (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: In Mexico City alone, Nahua towns organize 700 festivities a year, most honoring the patron saints of towns and neighborhoods, and mayordomías are in charge of organizing them.

source.title: Pueblos Nahuas : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Ñuu Savi
nations.lands: La Mixteca, in northwestern Oaxaca, southern Puebla and eastern Guerrero, Mexico, with migrant communities across Mexico and in the United States

facts.text: La Voz de la Mixteca, an INPI station in Tlaxiaco, Oaxaca, serves Mixtec, Triqui and Chocholtec peoples and has streamed online since 2006, reaching migrants in the United States.

source.title: XETLA La Voz de la Mixteca (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Palm weaving holds a special place in the Mixteca economy: artisans make hats, mats, purses, toys and brooms, and children start learning crafts around age six.

source.title: Mixtecos (Guerrero, Oaxaca y Puebla) : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Nn'anncue
nations.lands: The Sierra of the Costa Chica on the Guerrero and Oaxaca border, Mexico, including Xochistlahuaca, San Pedro Amuzgos and Santa María Ipalapa

facts.text: After a struggle that began in 1920, Amuzgo lands were restored as an ejido on August 25, 1933, covering 6,384 hectares.

source.title: Amuzgos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

facts.text: Amuzgo women weave huipiles, rebozos and tablecloths on the backstrap loom, while men make bamboo and palm baskets.

source.title: Amuzgos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Kitsé Cha'tnio
nations.lands: Southwestern Oaxaca, Mexico, near the Pacific coast, including Juquila, Yaitepec, Quiahije and Nopala

facts.text: Since 1994, La Voz de la Costa Chica in Santiago Jamiltepec, Oaxaca has broadcast in Mixtec, Amuzgo, Chatino, Tacuate and Spanish.

source.title: XEJAM La Voz de la Costa Chica (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Chatino weaving and embroidery continue in Yaitepec, Quiahije and Nopala, where blouses, shoulder bags, sashes and tablecloths are made.

source.title: Chatinos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: O' de püt
nations.lands: Northwestern and central Chiapas, Mexico, including Copainalá, Ocotepec, Tapalapa, Tecpatán, Ocozocoautla and Tuxtla Gutiérrez

facts.text: Since 1997, the INPI station La Voz de los Vientos has broadcast from Copainalá, a town whose Zoque name is Pokiomä, in Zoque, Tsotsil and Spanish.

source.title: XECOPA La Voz de los Vientos (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: In Ocotepec, Zoque artisans make wacas, vine baskets for washing coffee and cacao beans, sold through the Casa de las Artesanías de Chiapas.

source.title: Zoques : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Gwich'in
nations.lands: Northeast Alaska, including Fort Yukon, Venetie and Arctic Village, plus northern Yukon and the Northwest Territories in Canada

facts.text: Dinjii Zhuh K'yaa, the Gwich'in language, is one of ten Doyon region languages for which Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons.
Gwich'in Council International represents about 9,000 Gwich'in in Alaska, Yukon and the Northwest Territories as a Permanent Participant in the Arctic Council.

nations.name: St. Lawrence Island Yupik
nations.lands: Gambell and Savoonga on St. Lawrence Island in the Bering Sea, Alaska, United States; close relatives live on the Chukchi Peninsula across the Bering Strait

facts.text: St. Lawrence Island Yupik is almost the same language as the one spoken just across the Bering Strait, at the tip of Siberia's Chukchi Peninsula.

source.title: Languages - Siberian Yupik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

facts.text: The Alaska Native Language Center reports that children in Gambell and Savoonga learn St. Lawrence Island Yupik as the first language of the home.

source.title: Languages - Siberian Yupik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Unangax̂
nations.lands: Aleutian Islands, Pribilof Islands and the western Alaska Peninsula, Alaska, United States

facts.text: Students in APIA's 2025 Unangam Tunuu Summer Language Intensive learned from Unangax̂ Elders, and APIA holds a weekly Unangam Tunuu Community Night in Anchorage.
Unangam Tunuu is a single language with eastern and western dialects that divide at Atka Island.

source.title: Languages - Unangam Tunuu / Aleut
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Haida
nations.lands: Southern Prince of Wales Island, including Hydaburg, Kasaan and Craig, and Ketchikan, Southeast Alaska, United States

facts.text: Kasaan's 'Láa Náay Justice System works to keep the peace and promote wellness by addressing problems through culturally appropriate methods.
The Organized Village of Kasaan, a Haida tribal government, works to promote, preserve and protect Haida identity and values for its elders and youth.

nations.name: Tsimshian
nations.lands: Metlakatla on the Annette Islands Reserve, Southeast Alaska, United States; Tsimshian homelands continue in British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: The Hyaak Foundation in Metlakatla works to keep Sm'algyax, the Tsimshian language, alive and well.
The Metlakatla Indian Community on the Annette Islands holds the only Indian reserve in Alaska.

nations.name: Lower Tanana Dene
nations.lands: Nenana, Minto and the Fairbanks area along the Tanana River, Interior Alaska, United States

facts.text: Benhti Kenaga', the Lower Tanana language, is one of ten Doyon region languages for which Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons.
A pocket dictionary of the Lower Tanana language, which is spoken in Nenana and Minto on the Tanana River, was published in 2009.

source.title: Languages - Tanana
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Deg Hit'an
nations.lands: Shageluk, Anvik and Holy Cross on the lower Yukon River, Alaska, United States

facts.text: Deg Xinag is one of ten Doyon region languages for which Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons.
Learners can use a free online Deg Xinag dictionary with sound recordings, available through the Alaska Native Knowledge Network.

source.title: Languages - Deg Xinag
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Native Village of Eklutna
nations.lands: Alaska; the Tribal government describes community work in Eklutna Village and Anchorage

facts.text: The Tribe describes its government as traditional rather than formed under the Indian Reorganization Act, with seven Council members serving staggered three-year terms.
The Tribe reports working with partners on assessment, planning and restoration of the Eklutna River. The page describes ongoing work, not a completed restoration.

nations.name: Native Hawaiians
nations.lands: The Hawaiian Islands (Hawaiʻi), United States

facts.text: The Office of Hawaiian Affairs, approved by Hawaiʻi voters in 1978 to serve Native Hawaiians, is governed by nine trustees elected statewide for four-year terms.
Since a 1978 amendment to the state constitution, Hawaiian and English have both been official languages of the State of Hawaiʻi.

source.title: State Constitution
source.publisher: Legislative Reference Bureau, State of Hawaiʻi

nations.name: Eyak
nations.lands: Cordova, the Copper River Delta and Prince William Sound, Alaska, United States

facts.text: The Native Village of Eyak in Cordova is a federally recognized tribe that unites Eyak, Chugach Region, Tlingit and Athabaskan peoples.

source.title: Native Village of Eyak - About Us

facts.text: Eyak is not an Athabascan language but its own branch beside the Athabascan languages, within the Athabascan-Eyak-Tlingit language family.

source.title: Languages - Eyak
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Yup'ik
nations.lands: Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and nearby coasts and rivers of southwest Alaska, United States

facts.text: In the Calista Region along the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers, subsistence hunting, fishing and gathering bind communities together and are part of who people are.
The word Yup'ik names both the language and the people, built from yuk, meaning person, and pik, meaning real.

source.title: Languages - Central Yup'ik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Kággaba
nations.lands: Northern, eastern and western slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in La Guajira, Magdalena and Cesar, Colombia

facts.text: The Organización Gonawindúa Tayrona serves as the representative body of the Kággaba people's own Indigenous government.
The Kággaba speak their own language, often called Kogui, which belongs to the Chibcha language family.

source.title: Kaggabba (Kogui): los guardianes de la armonía del mundo
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Quechua
nations.lands: Andean highlands and valleys of Peru and Bolivia, with Quechua communities also in Argentina and Chile

facts.text: Peru's Ministry of Culture lists Quechua as a vital language, and the 2017 census counted 3,805,531 people who learned to speak it in childhood.

source.title: Quechuas | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: Peru's Ministry of Culture reports that 5,179,774 people nationwide feel or consider themselves part of the Quechua peoples.

source.title: Quechuas | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Diaguita
nations.lands: Huasco and Choapa valleys of Chile's Norte Chico, and northwestern Argentina

facts.text: The first Diaguita community constituted under Chile's Indigenous Law, the Estancia Agrícola Diaguita de los Huascoaltinos, formed in 2006.
Many people who self-identify as Diaguita in Chile live in the upper Huasco River basin, in the municipality of Alto del Carmen.

nations.name: Kichwa Otavalo
nations.lands: Otavalo and nearby communities such as Peguche in Imbabura province, northern Ecuador

facts.text: Hampiriypacha, a Kichwa Otavalo association of seed guardians, works to protect knowledge that women have passed down for generations.

source.title: Meet our 2022 Keepers of the Earth Fund Grant Partners

facts.text: Yarina, a Kichwa Otavalo family band started in 1984, plays original Indigenous rhythms on traditional Andean instruments and works to keep Kichwa traditions alive.

nations.name: Kichwa Puruwá
nations.lands: Chimborazo province in the central highlands of Ecuador

facts.text: The Puruwá people include the communities of Cacha, Colta, Licto and Guamote in Chimborazo, each with its own local character.

source.title: Guía Nacional de Nutrición de las Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas, Afroecuatoriano y Montubio
source.publisher: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador

facts.text: Ecuador's 2010 census counted 136,141 Kichwa Puruwá people, about 18.5 percent of the whole Kichwa nationality.

source.title: Guía Nacional de Nutrición de las Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas, Afroecuatoriano y Montubio
source.publisher: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador

nations.name: Nasa
nations.lands: Cauca department, especially Tierradentro and northern Cauca, with communities in Huila, Valle del Cauca, Tolima and Putumayo, Colombia

facts.text: In 1971 Indigenous communities of Cauca founded the CRIC to recover resguardo lands, strengthen their cabildos and defend their history, language and customs.

source.title: Nasa (Paez), la gente del agua
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: The Nasa language is Nasa Yuwe. In Colombia's 2005 census, 41.9 percent of Nasa people reported speaking it.

source.title: Nasa (Paez), la gente del agua
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Aymara
nations.lands: The altiplano around Lake Titicaca and nearby valleys and cities of Bolivia and Peru, and the far north of Chile

facts.text: Aymara is a vital language in Peru, where the 2017 census counted 450,010 people who learned to speak it in childhood.

source.title: Aimara | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: In Bolivia's 2024 census, more than one million people self-identified as Aymara, and more than one million as Quechua.

source.title: INE presenta resultados del Censo 2024 que muestran la transformación demográfica y avances sociales en Bolivia
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística de Bolivia

nations.name: Wiwa
nations.lands: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in La Guajira, Cesar and Magdalena, Colombia

facts.text: Most young Wiwa speak three languages: Damana, their mother tongue, the neighboring Kogui language, and Spanish.

source.title: Wiwa: la gente que da origen al calor
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: Through education policies the Wiwa established an alphabet for Damana, and they are working to have it taught alongside Spanish in schools.

source.title: Wiwa: la gente que da origen al calor
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Kichwa Kañari
nations.lands: Cañar and Azuay provinces in the southern highlands of Ecuador

facts.text: In Cañar parish, the province's largest Indigenous organizational network brings together 15 communities and 5 cooperatives.

source.title: Guía Nacional de Nutrición de las Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas, Afroecuatoriano y Montubio
source.publisher: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador

facts.text: The Kañari keep a vigorous ethnic identity and a very strong organizational system, in which cooperatives and many kinds of organizations are very active.

source.title: Guía Nacional de Nutrición de las Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas, Afroecuatoriano y Montubio
source.publisher: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador

nations.name: Misak
nations.lands: Resguardos of Guambía and Quisgó in Silvia, Cauca, and nearby municipalities of southwestern Colombia

facts.text: The Misak keep their mother tongue, Wampi-misamerawam, and see it as central to their ethnic and cultural identity.

source.title: Misak (Guambianos), la gente del agua, del conocimiento y de los sueños
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: In 2000 a Misak leader became the first Indigenous person elected by popular vote as governor of Colombia's Cauca department.

source.title: Misak (Guambianos), la gente del agua, del conocimiento y de los sueños
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Kichwa Kayambi
nations.lands: Around Cayambe in Pichincha province and neighboring areas of Imbabura, northern Ecuador

facts.text: In 2022 Kayambi water boards, communes and community organizations met with a national legislator to discuss issues including a new water law.

source.title: Asamblea ampliada y mesa de trabajo con el Pueblo Kayambi

facts.text: The Confederación del Pueblo Kayambi holds a General Assembly where its communities and organizations bring their proposals and demands.

source.title: Asamblea General con el Pueblo Kayambi

nations.name: Mansi
nations.lands: Ob and Irtysh basin in western Siberia, mainly Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug (Yugra), with small groups in Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Okrug and Sverdlovsk Oblast, Russia

facts.text: Luima Seripos, a newspaper in the Mansi language, first came out on 11 February 1989 and is still produced today in a joint newsroom with the Khanty paper.

source.title: Историческая справка
source.publisher: Khanty Mansi Mir (joint editorial office of the Khanty Yasang and Luima Seripos newspapers)

facts.text: Mansi rapper Yevgeny Anyamov, known as Bizzo, records his songs in Mansi and opened his own studio in his hometown of Ivdel to share his people's culture with youth.

nations.name: Nivkh
nations.lands: Lower Amur River in Khabarovsk Krai and Sakhalin Island, Russia

facts.text: The Nivkh speak a language isolate, probably one of the oldest languages of Eurasia. Its links to other languages have not been established.

source.title: Нивхи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Nivkh life was built on fishing and hunting, including sea mammals taken with spears or with nets woven from leather straps.

source.title: Нивхи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Luoravetlan
nations.lands: Chukotka Autonomous Okrug, northern Kamchatka Krai and the Nizhnekolymsky District of Sakha (Yakutia), Russia

facts.text: Researchers at Russia's Kunstkamera museum published a 2018 study on the mobile dwellings of Chukchi reindeer herders, covering both traditions and innovations.

source.title: Arctic Research Center
source.publisher: Peter the Great Museum of Anthropology and Ethnography (Kunstkamera), Russian Academy of Sciences

facts.text: Carving bone and walrus ivory and embroidering with reindeer hair are long-standing Chukchi arts, practised alongside reindeer herding and hunting.

source.title: Чукчи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Even
nations.lands: Northeastern Siberia: Sakha (Yakutia), Magadan Oblast, Kamchatka, Chukotka and Khabarovsk Krai, Russia

facts.text: The Even language belongs to the Tungusic (Manchu-Tungus) branch and is close to Evenki. Even self-names include Even (local) and Orochel (reindeer people).

source.title: Эвены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: The 2002 census counted 11,657 Even living in the Republic of Sakha (Yakutia).

source.title: Эвены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Itelmen
nations.lands: Tigilsky District on the west coast of Kamchatka Krai, with smaller groups in Chukotka and Magadan Oblast, Russia

facts.text: Western Itelmen is the Itelmen language that has been kept to the present day.

source.title: Ительмены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Fishing, above all for salmon, is the traditional Itelmen livelihood on Kamchatka.

source.title: Ительмены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Ket
nations.lands: Yenisei River basin, mainly Turukhansky District of Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia

facts.text: A Cyrillic writing system that Ket speakers actually use came into being in the late 1980s.

source.title: Кеты
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Ket is the only living language of the Yeniseian language family.

source.title: Кеты
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Inughuit
nations.lands: Avanersuaq (the Thule region) in northwest Greenland, centred on the town of Qaanaaq

facts.text: Hunting is still a significant part of the livelihood of several families in Qaanaaq, Greenland's youngest and northernmost town.
The Inughuit have their own language, or dialect, and a hunting culture that is distinctive in several ways.

nations.name: Yupik
nations.lands: Settlements on the eastern coast of the Chukchi Peninsula, Chukotka Autonomous Okrug, Russia, across the Bering Strait from Alaska

facts.text: Inuit from Chukotka became part of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in 1992, a goal that was in ICC's vision from the very beginning.
Yupik hunters are regarded as originators of traditional whaling in the region, hunting walrus, seal and whale with harpoons.

source.title: Эскимосы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Evenki
nations.lands: Siberian taiga from the Ob River to the Sea of Okhotsk, with the largest group in Sakha (Yakutia), also Krasnoyarsk and Khabarovsk krais, Buryatia, Amur, Irkutsk and Zabaykalsky regions of Russia, and in China and Mongolia

facts.text: Evenki communities live across Russia, with the largest in Sakha (Yakutia), and Evenki also live in China and Mongolia.

source.title: Эвенки
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Evenki homelands span a huge part of the Siberian taiga, from the Ob River in the west to the Sea of Okhotsk in the east.

source.title: The Evenks
source.publisher: The Red Book of the Peoples of the Russian Empire (Institute of the Estonian Language archive)

nations.name: Dolgan
nations.lands: Taimyr Peninsula in Krasnoyarsk Krai (Taimyr Dolgan-Nenets District) and the Anabar District and city of Yakutsk in Sakha (Yakutia), Russia

facts.text: During an August 2026 folk culture expedition to Khatanga, the Dolgan dried-fish dish kerdiileek was added to the list of Taimyr's intangible cultural heritage.

source.title: Долганская юкола «кэрдиилээк» признана объектом нематериального наследия Таймыра
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Dolgan is a Turkic language, close to Sakha (Yakut), from which it separated through isolated development.

source.title: Долганы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Wajãpi
nations.lands: Wajãpi Indigenous Land in Amapá, Brazil, and the middle and upper Oyapock River in French Guiana

facts.text: In 1994 the Wajãpi began demarcating their own Indigenous Land in Amapá, Brazil, and founded the Council of Wajãpi Villages, known as Apina.

source.title: Wajãpi
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

facts.text: In French Guiana the Wayãpi live along the middle and upper Oyapock River.

nations.name: Wayana
nations.lands: Upper Maroni River and its tributaries in French Guiana, the Tapanahony and Paloemeu rivers in Suriname, and the East Paru River in Pará, Brazil

facts.text: France recognizes Wayana as one of six Amerindian languages of French Guiana with the status of a language of France.

source.title: Langues de France et langues régionales en Guyane: bilan au 7 décembre 2015
source.publisher: Ministère de la Culture, Direction des affaires culturelles de Guyane

facts.text: Among younger people on Brazil's East Paru River, the Wayana language has gained great prestige.

source.title: Wayana
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

nations.name: Uwottüja
nations.lands: The Autana, Cuao, Sipapo and Guayapo rivers and the middle Orinoco, Amazonas state, Venezuela

facts.text: In 2020 Uwottüja communities of the Autana, Cuao, Sipapo and Guayapo rivers met at Pendare and declared themselves guardians of their territory.

source.title: Pronunciamiento del Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja de los habitantes de los cuatro ríos Autana, Cuao, Sipapo, Guayapo y el sector Orinoco Medio
source.publisher: Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja, published by the Observatorio de Ecología Política de Venezuela

facts.text: The Uwottüja held their first congress as a people in 1984, uniting around the defense of their ancestral lands 'like one churuata, with one voice'.

source.title: Pronunciamiento del Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja de los habitantes de los cuatro ríos Autana, Cuao, Sipapo, Guayapo y el sector Orinoco Medio
source.publisher: Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja, published by the Observatorio de Ecología Política de Venezuela

nations.name: Ye'kwana
nations.lands: Amazonas and Bolívar states in southern Venezuela, and the Auaris and Uraricoera rivers of Roraima, Brazil

facts.text: The name Ye'kwana, which the people use for themselves, entered Venezuela's census in 1982 and has almost fully replaced the outside name Makiritare.

source.title: Censo Nacional de Población y Vivienda 2011: Empadronamiento de la Población Indígena

facts.text: Among themselves the Ye'kwana use So'to, meaning 'people', while Ye'kwana can be translated as 'canoe people'.

source.title: Ye'kwana
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

nations.name: Teko
nations.lands: Camopi on the Oyapock River and Cayodé on the upper Maroni, French Guiana

facts.text: France lists Teko, formerly called Émerillon, among French Guiana's six Amerindian languages recognized as languages of France.

source.title: Langues de France et langues régionales en Guyane: bilan au 7 décembre 2015
source.publisher: Ministère de la Culture, Direction des affaires culturelles de Guyane

facts.text: Teko and Wayãpi are the two Tupi-Guarani languages spoken in the Amazonian Park of French Guiana, where Wayana belongs to the Carib family.

nations.name: Pemón
nations.lands: Savannas of southeastern Venezuela, the Kamarang River area of Guyana, and Roraima state in Brazil

facts.text: Taurepang, Arekuna and Kamarakoto communities share the self-name Pemon, a word meaning 'people' or 'us'.

source.title: Taurepang
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

facts.text: In Guyana, Arekuna communities live on the banks of the Kamarang River.

source.title: Indigenous Nations
source.publisher: Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, Government of Guyana

nations.name: Akawaio
nations.lands: Upper Mazaruni area and nearby river valleys of western Guyana, with Akawaio also counted in Venezuela's census

facts.text: Akawaio is one of the nine Indigenous languages covered by Guyana's language revival programme, which the government moved to restart in 2021.

source.title: Gov't to resume Amerindian language revival project
source.publisher: Department of Public Information, Government of Guyana

facts.text: Kapohn is the Akawaio people's own name for themselves, and like most peoples of Guyana's interior they are Carib speakers.

nations.name: Barí
nations.lands: Serranía de los Motilones and the Catatumbo and Oro river basins in Norte de Santander, Colombia, and Zulia state, Venezuela

facts.text: The Barí language, of the Chibcha family, is being passed on to new generations and has speakers of all ages.
Barí live in the foothills of Colombia's Serranía de los Motilones along the Catatumbo and Oro rivers, with settlements also in Zulia state, Venezuela.
